newsitem.title: GERMANY: Poll says German majority expects EMU on time.
newsitem.headline: Poll says German majority expects EMU on time.

text.p: Fifty-four percent of Germans surveyed in the Allensbach Institute's latest monthly poll said they expected Europe's monetary union (EMU) to start on time even though 52 percent said they were against it.

Only 22 percent said they supported the single currency, a core item of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's political agenda. Thirty-one percent said they did not expect EMU on time while 15 percent were undecided.
"We cannot expect strong swings in the public's attitude on this anymore," Allensbach director Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann wrote in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Wednesday.

"Public opinion on this has basically been the same for the past year," she wrote. "The excitement about Finance Minister (Theo) Waigel's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves probably only strengthened people in their feeling that the debates about monetary union are completely incomprehensible."
The poll was taken from April 22 to May 2, before Waigel sparked off an uproar by trying to get the central bank to revalue its gold stocks to help him fill budget gaps this year to qualify for EMU.

Thirty-six percent of Germans polled told Allensbach they thought EMU would bring the European Union closer together, eight percent said it would push EU countries apart and 43 percent expected no change.
Thirty-nine percent expected EMU to have no effect on economic growth in the EU while 24 percent expected higher growth and 18 percent foresaw a lower rate.
But almost a majority -- 48 percent -- expected higher inflation compared to seven percent expecting lower inflation and 23 percent seeing no change.
On unemployment, 45 percent saw it unchanged under EMU while 35 percent expected it to grow and 10 percent thought it would fall.
Asked if they would like to turn back the wheel of history and abolish the EU, 55 percent said no and only 18 percent said yes. Twenty-seven percent were undecided.
